H1.title: Opportunity Cost of Motherhood
H1.theory: Female education and labor force participation raise the career penalty of children, reducing TFR. But the relationship may be nonlinear — at high gender equity, the effect partially reverses.

evidence.reasoning: Key variables statistically significant (p<0.05); Large cross-country sample (214 countries); Direct measurement of key concept

H2.title: Housing Affordability Trap
H2.theory: Housing cost-to-income ratio delays family formation. One study attributes 51% of the U.S. fertility decline to rising housing costs.

evidence.reasoning: Key variables statistically significant (p<0.05); Small sample (12 countries) — results may not generalize; Poor proxy for key concept (gov consumption/GDP is a poor proxy for actual housing costs); Limited data coverage

H2.note: IMPORTANT LIMITATION: Our "housing_cost_proxy" is government consumption as % of GDP — NOT actual housing prices or rent-to-income ratios. This is a weak proxy at best. The academic evidence (using actual housing data) is stronger than what we can show here. Only 12 countries available.

H3.title: Cultural Sticky Equilibria (Low Fertility Trap)
H3.theory: Once TFR drops below ~1.5, intergenerational norm transmission locks in low fertility. Recovery is extremely difficult.

evidence.reasoning: Key variables statistically significant (p<0.05); Large cross-country sample (71 countries); Direct measurement of key concept

H3.note: The regression tests whether TFR change is more negative when below 1.5 (mean reversion + trap stickiness). The descriptive statistic (86% of countries that fell below 1.5 have NOT recovered to 1.7) is the more compelling evidence — but this could partly reflect mean reversion dynamics rather than a cultural trap per se.

H4.title: Secularization
H4.theory: Societal-level religiosity decline predicts TFR decline. Very religious individuals in secular societies have fewer children than equivalent individuals in religious societies.

evidence.reasoning: Key variables statistically significant (p<0.05); Small sample (12 countries) — results may not generalize; Reasonable proxy for key concept; Limited data coverage

H4.note: Limited to 12 countries with religiosity index data. With only 12 countries, statistical power is very low — a non-significant result here does NOT disprove the hypothesis. The GSS micro-evidence (religious Americans have more children) is consistent with the theory even if the macro regression lacks power.

H5.title: Partnership Decline
H5.theory: Declining marriage and cohabitation rates mechanically reduce aggregate fertility. Since 2001, marital status changes explain most of the fertility decline in several countries.

evidence.reasoning: Key variables statistically significant (p<0.05); Large cross-country sample (231 countries); Poor proxy for key concept (urbanization is a very indirect proxy for marriage/partnership rates)

H5.note: CRITICAL LIMITATION: We have NO direct marriage or partnership rate data in our panel. Urbanization is used as a very rough proxy. The GSS micro-evidence (dramatic shift from married to never-married, with large fertility differences by marital status) provides much stronger support for this hypothesis than the macro regression.

H6.title: Economic Uncertainty / Pessimism
H6.theory: Not just income levels but economic uncertainty (policy uncertainty, inflation volatility, consumer pessimism) suppresses fertility intentions and realization.

models.name: H6a: Global EPU (entity FE only — cannot use year FE)

evidence.reasoning: Key variables statistically significant (p<0.05); Large cross-country sample (234 countries); Direct measurement of key concept

H6.note: Global EPU is constant across countries within a year, so it is absorbed by year fixed effects. We show it with entity FE only (which risks time-trend confounding). Country-specific EPU (12 countries only) can use two-way FE. The honest interpretation: EPU effects are hard to separate from the common downward time trend in TFR.

H7.title: J-Curve Reversal (Contested)
H7.theory: At very high HDI (>0.86), further development may increase fertility, reversing the traditional negative relationship. Myrskylä et al. (2009) claimed this; later research disputes it.

evidence.reasoning: Key variables statistically significant (p<0.05); Small sample (12 countries) — results may not generalize; Poor proxy for key concept (HDI proxy computed from components — not official UNDP HDI)

H7.note: The J-curve claim is highly contested in the literature. Our HDI proxy is computed from education, life expectancy, and GDP components — NOT official UNDP HDI values. HDI also heavily overlaps with H1 variables (education, GDP). Even if the quadratic term is significant, it could reflect compositional effects rather than a true reversal.

H8.title: Policy Effectiveness Ceiling
H8.theory: Pro-natalist policies (childcare subsidies, parental leave) have modest positive effects but diminishing returns, especially below TFR ~1.5.

evidence.reasoning: Key variables statistically significant (p<0.05); Small sample (8 countries) — results may not generalize; Direct measurement of key concept; Limited data coverage

H8.note: Limited to 12 countries with OECD-style policy data. Policy endogeneity is a serious concern: countries with LOW TFR adopt MORE family spending (reverse causality). This biases the coefficient toward zero or even negative.

H9.title: Smartphone / Social Media Effect
H9.theory: Algorithmic social media content amplifies fertility anxiety and displaces relationship formation. The post-2010 fertility decline in developed countries coincides with smartphone adoption.

evidence.reasoning: Key variables statistically significant (p<0.05); Large cross-country sample (228 countries); Poor proxy for key concept (internet/mobile penetration is proxy for social media — not direct measure)

H9.note: The post_smartphone dummy is absorbed by year FE (it's the same for all countries in a given year). The interaction (internet × post_smartphone) survives two-way FE because it varies across countries. However, internet penetration also proxies for general development — so the "smartphone effect" may partly reflect development trends.

random_forest.note: RF does NOT use fixed effects — it uses raw (non-demeaned) data. Feature importance reflects both between-country and within-country variation. This means high-importance variables may be important for explaining cross-country differences rather than within-country changes over time.

projection_params.note: Projection uses entity FE only (not two-way FE) since we are projecting forward and year effects are not available for future years. This is a simple linear sensitivity analysis, not a forecast.
